# Boundary response: rank and basis transfer {#sec-boundary-response}

**After the exact principal part is removed, the Laplace boundary response of
a 2D geometry is low-rank and resolution-stable, but the singular vectors of
that residual are geometry-specific: a basis fitted on smooth bodies and
wide-gap pairs misses narrow gaps, thin annuli and corners by one to two
orders of magnitude at equal rank.** The audit's second direction proposed
learning the geometry-dependent boundary response with its known singular
structure removed, and predicted that the difficult residual modes would
track topology and near interactions. The nonlearned gate confirms the
compressibility half and rejects the transfer half as posed.

## The gate {#sec-boundary-gate}

Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) operators of the interior Laplace problem on
closed 2D curves, assembled by a Nyström boundary-integral discretization
(Kress quadrature for the logarithmic kernel, trapezoid double layer,
arclength resampling), qualified against the unit-disk DtN (exact to 10⁻¹³
on every mode), the annulus (log r fluxes exact to four digits), a two-body
flux identity (2 × 10⁻¹³) and a resolution doubling on every geometry
(22 of 23 converged to 10⁻⁸; one star excluded). Families: ellipses and
stars (smooth single bodies), two-body pairs with gap-to-length ratio from
0.5 to 0.02, annuli with inner radius 0.3 to 0.85, and rounded squares
with corner radius from 0.14 to 0.016 of the side. Principal part: the
arclength-Fourier symbol |k| per component; component constants (the DtN
null space) removed explicitly. Readouts: the rank needed for 1% (and 0.1%)
relative Frobenius error by the full operator, by the residual after the
principal part, and after constants too, in both the L2 and the energy
pairing; and the projection error of a basis fitted on the source
development set (single bodies plus wide-gap pairs) on each held-out family
at that family's oracle rank. Bars, written before the run
(`studies/boundary_response/PREREG.md`): worth a learner if the residual
reaches 1% at no more than a third of the full rank on the held-out
families AND the source-fitted basis is within 2x of the oracle basis at
that rank.

## What the gate found {#sec-boundary-result}

| family | nodes | full operator | residual after principal part | after constants | residual share of the operator (L2 / energy) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ellipses (aspect 1.5 / 2 / 3) | 192 | 184 | 8 / 12 / 20 | same | 0.001–0.003 / 0.03–0.12 |
| stars (five qualified) | 512 | 489 | 12–32 | same | ≤ 0.001 / 0.02–0.07 |
| pairs, gap 0.5 / 0.3 (source) | 768 | 733 | 16 / 19 | 16 / 18 | 0.001 / 0.07–0.09 |
| pairs, gap 0.2 / 0.1 / 0.05 / 0.02 | 1,024–1,536 | 977–1,467 | 22 / 29 / 38 / 58 | 21 / 28 / 37 / 56 | 0.001–0.008 / 0.11–0.44 |
| annuli, inner radius 0.3 / 0.6 / 0.85 | 384 / 384 / 768 | 361 / 369 / 740 | 20 / 50 / 160 | 21 / 50 / 160 | 0.002–0.014 / 0.14–0.62 |
| rounded squares, corner radius 0.14 → 0.016 | 256–1,024 | 245–977 | 16 / 24 / 32 / 39 | same | ≤ 0.002 / 0.03–0.05 |

: Rank for 1% self-relative Frobenius error (L2 pairing); identical at
double resolution for every qualified geometry. Data:
`studies/boundary_response/results.json`. {#tbl-boundary-rank}

The residual is low-rank everywhere: 2.5–7% of the full rank for narrow
gaps and corners, with the thin annulus the worst case at 22% (11% in the
energy pairing). The rank grows with narrowing gaps roughly as
(g/L)^−0.4, and the residual's share of the operator grows faster (7% to
44% of the energy norm from gap 0.5 to 0.02), so the principal part
explains less of the operator exactly where geometry matters most. The
energy pairing lowers the ranks by 25–45%, and about 98% of the operator's
squared Frobenius norm lives in modes above N/4, which is the audit's
spectrum point (wall flux is dominated by modes that interior values barely
see) made quantitative.

| pairing / object | held-out family | oracle basis error | source-fitted basis error | ratio, median / worst |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| energy / residual | gaps (16 blocks) | 0.007 | 0.31 | 46 / 70 |
| energy / residual | annuli (12) | 0.009 | 0.063 | 7 / 33 |
| energy / residual | corners (4) | 0.008 | 0.25 | 34 / 61 |
| L2 / residual | gaps / annuli / corners | 0.009 | 0.74 / 0.23 / 0.56 | 83 / 25 / 64 |

: Projection error at each held-out block's oracle 1% rank; the bar was a
ratio of 2. Random-probe readouts agree within 0.01. {#tbl-boundary-transfer}

The source-fitted basis fails by one to two orders of magnitude on every
held-out family; to reach 1% it needs rank 30 / 78 / 50 (annuli / corners /
gaps, medians) against oracle ranks of 13 / 22 / 9, and up to 64–96 of 97
modes in the worst blocks, which is no compression at all.

## What this changes {#sec-boundary-consequence}

The preregistered outcome is partial, and the informative half is the
failure. A compressible residual exists for each geometry, so a learner has
something small to produce; but the residual's basis does not transfer, so
the direction cannot be "a fixed basis with geometry-conditioned
coefficients". If it continues, the learner must be a geometry-to-operator
map that produces a rank-r residual in component-local coordinates with
explicit coupling blocks, with the principal part built in exactly, trained
and graded in the energy pairing (where the residual is a sized object,
3–62% of the operator), with thin gaps and thin shells as the held-out
family. The cheap next nonlearned test is a coordinate question, whether a
curvature-indexed basis transfers better than a Fourier-indexed one, and it
should precede any training. Two limits stand: no arclength-Fourier basis
exists on 3D surfaces, so the principal part would have to be derived from
the surface metric there; and nothing here touches Navier–Stokes, where the
potential-flow prior already failed on separated cars.
